title: WISP 00: WISP process and document format
implementation: Process proposal
summary: Separate Ghost, the small rendezvous primitive, from Ghostly, its reference application, and make independently implementable extensions reviewable. WISP is the working document name; this draft does not decide its expanded acronym.
benefit: How a WISP is written, reviewed and numbered, and what Draft, Proposed and Final mean.

title: WISP 01: Ghost Core Protocol
implementation: Rendezvous and DHT text in every client; the DHT as rendezvous and floor of every chat; native clients (Desktop, CLI) read the Mainline DHT directly; a circuit breaker per Pkarr relay in every client
summary: Ghost is layer 0 of every 1:1 chat (400). It is always the rendezvous: where the invite's keys meet, where the first contact and handshake happen (403), where each side publishes its presence, its capability record (03) and the signaling or descriptors a peer-to-peer transport needs (100). It is also the floor: when no peer-to-peer transport connects, or the one in use drops, short text and its receipts travel in bou
benefit: Find a peer through small signed records on the Mainline DHT, without turning discovery into storage.
note: The rendezvous exists since the first release; the modular boundary is a proposal.

title: WISP 02: Peer Keys
implementation: Existing per-link keys; lifecycle extensions proposed
summary: The follow-up adds transcript-negotiated signed signaling, durable per-message delivery/retry state and observed extension interoperability; see the implementation profile for exact partial coverage and residual risks. This does not change Draft status.
benefit: A fresh identity for every connection, and pinning the key of the person you paired with.

title: WISP 03: Capability Negotiation
implementation: Existing advertisements and the paired pair-offer; the layer-0 capability record in every new chat
summary: The one chat of 400 negotiates capabilities in two places:
benefit: Both sides announce versioned abilities and only use what they have in common.
note: Every new chat announces its abilities in a record on the DHT before a live link exists, then agrees on them on the live link. Chats with Ghostly 0.4 contacts keep a fixed set.

title: WISP 04: Local Profiles
implementation: Experimental: web, desktop and browser extension clients
summary: A profile is a local container on one device. It holds everything a person may want to keep apart (for example "Personal" and "Work"), and exactly one profile is active in a running client. A profile is not a protocol identity: contacts never learn that profiles exist, how many there are, or their names. Each chat already has its own keys (02); a profile groups chats and everything tied to them.
benefit: Keep separate lives on one device (chats, wallets, services and settings), never announced to contacts.
note: Web, desktop and extension. Switch from the account bar in one tap.

title: WISP 05: Profile Backups
implementation: Experimental: web, desktop and browser extension clients
summary: A profile backup captures one local profile (04) completely, so it can be brought back on this or another device: chats and their keys, messages and files, wallets and their payment journal, shared services and grants, per-chat payment choices and settings. It is one opaque, encrypted bundle. Where a bundle is kept (a file, an S3 bucket) is the concern of storage adapters (1000); this document defines what a bundle i
benefit: Bring a whole profile back from one passphrase-sealed bundle.
note: Web, desktop and extension. A restore always creates a new profile; nothing is overwritten.

title: WISP 100: Transport Negotiation
implementation: Experimental: rank-sum negotiation, the DHT floor, background retry and upgrade in every new chat; relayed transports; a choice made while not live travels in the capability record
summary: Every 1:1 chat of 400 has two layers. Layer 0 is the DHT: the rendezvous, and the floor that carries short text (403) when nothing else connects. Layer 1 is the transport this document selects: WebRTC (101), Iroh (102) or HyperDHT (103).
benefit: Pick a data path both peers support, in order of preference; fall back only when both allow it.

title: WISP 1000: Storage Contract
implementation: Experimental: local file (1001) and S3-compatible (1002) adapters
summary: Storage keeps encrypted bundles (05) somewhere other than the running profile: a file the person holds, a bucket, later a WebDAV share or a relay. The 10xx family defines one contract that every place implements, so backups, and later continuity features, do not depend on any single provider. Storage never sees plaintext and never decides what a bundle contains.
benefit: Where sealed bundles are kept, separate from what goes into a backup.
note: Holds backups and, since store-and-forward, items sealed for an away contact.

title: WISP 1001: Local File Storage
implementation: Experimental: web, desktop and browser extension clients
summary: The simplest place: a file the person keeps. It needs no account, network or credential.
benefit: The simplest place: a file you keep. No account, no network.
note: Backups only: a file has no address to hand a contact, so it cannot hold messages.

title: WISP 1002: S3-Compatible Storage
implementation: Experimental: web and desktop clients; exercised against a local S3-compatible server
summary: Any service speaking the S3 object API: AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2, Wasabi, MinIO, Garage and others.
benefit: Any S3-compatible bucket (AWS, R2, B2, MinIO, Garage) holding only encrypted bundles.
note: Backups and held messages on every client. The bucket's CORS rules must allow the app (and GET from your contacts' apps, to hold).

title: WISP 101: WebRTC
implementation: Existing adapter in the web app, the extension and Desktop on macOS and Windows (Linux WebKitGTK has no WebRTC); WISP binding proposed
summary: WebRTC is one layer-1 candidate of the one chat (400, 100), and the only direct one in browsers and the extension (they reach Iroh, and HyperDHT when a relay is set, only through a relay: 102, 103). Its rtc signaling rides layer 0, in the link's own signed record, as today. A WebRTC attempt that does not connect (no ICE path, no TURN, a blocked network) no longer fails a first pairing: the chat stays on-dht and retri
benefit: Carry a session over a WebRTC data channel, the direct path browsers have.
note: Browser, extension and desktop, except Linux, whose webview has no WebRTC. May use STUN/TURN servers to get through networks.

title: WISP 102: Iroh
implementation: Experimental: native adapter of the chat session (desktop); relay-only browser build in the web app and the extension; endpoint id and home relay in the layer-0 capability record
summary: Iroh is a native layer-1 candidate of the one chat (400, 100). Its endpoint id is published in the layer-0 capability record (03), so two desktops try Iroh without a WebRTC session first. The endpoint id is dialled through Iroh's own discovery; no address goes into the record. An Iroh attempt that fails leaves the chat on-dht, and a dropped Iroh session sends it there until a transport is back.
benefit: Use an Iroh QUIC endpoint, with Ghostly authentication bound to the connection.
note: Experimental. Direct between desktop apps, tried from the first contact. The web app and extension use it through relays (n0's public ones unless you set others), so a web chat can reach a desktop.

title: WISP 103: HyperDHT
implementation: Experimental: native adapter of the chat session (desktop); browsers through a HyperDHT relay (web app, extension; off until a relay is set); public key in the layer-0 capability record
summary: HyperDHT is a native layer-1 candidate of the one chat (400, 100). Its DHT is not the chat's layer 0: layer 0 is Pkarr on the Mainline DHT, and a HyperDHT lookup is part of dialling this transport. Its public key is published in the layer-0 capability record (03), so it can be tried without a WebRTC session first. A failed attempt leaves the chat on-dht; a dropped session sends it there until a transport is back.
benefit: Use an authenticated Noise stream found through HyperDHT.
note: Experimental. Between desktop apps, tried from the first contact. The web app and extension reach it only through a relay you set: none runs by default.

title: WISP 11xx: Headless Runtime and Local Control API
implementation: Experimental: packages/cli (@ghostly/cli, command ghostly), phases 1 to 5 on dev; the npm package is not published
documentKind: Contract (local API; nothing here goes on the wire between peers)
summary: Bots talk through chats the way the Hermes agent does on Telegram: a process that stays online, reads what arrives, answers, pays and gets paid. For that, everything the app does has to be reachable without a screen. This document fixes how Ghostly runs headless (the runtime), how other programs on the same machine drive it (the local control API), and what it tells them (the event stream). It changes nothing between
benefit: Run Ghostly without a screen for a bot: a daemon keeps a profile online, a JSON event stream says what arrived, and the ghostly command answers, pays and shares.
note: Experimental, the same engine as the apps on Node: ghostly1 invites, chats (typing, replies, edits, reactions), groups, wallets, files and voice notes, identity proofs, shared apps, and voice calls whose audio a program of yours hears and speaks. Not on npm yet; no Bark or Fedimint wallets, no video in calls, and the DHT only through relays. Number not yet assigned.

title: WISP 200: Payment Negotiation
implementation: Payment frames with wallets per network (Mainnet and Testnet side by side); experimental rails: Cashu, Lightning cards, Ark (Arkade, Bark), Spark, Fedimint, USDT, on-chain Bitcoin
summary: Ghost negotiates payment methods and carries requests/results; it does not mandate a new wallet. Current pay-req, pay, pay-res frames use request/payment IDs, decimal-text amounts, an asset and ordered endpoints. Initial identifiers are cashu and btc-lightning-bolt11; the other rails add their own endpoints (btc-arkade/1, btc-bark/1, btc-spark/1, fedimint-ecash/1, btc-onchain/1, USDT). Frames run only over the data l
benefit: Agree on a payment method and carry the request; the wallet adapter moves the value.
note: Methods are negotiated in every chat, and in groups between two members. Any wallet can pay a request from its QR code or link; it is settled only when the payee's own wallet sees the money.

title: WISP 201: Cashu
implementation: Cashu wallet per network (Mainnet and Testnet); shared reviewed-payment coordinator
summary: Ghostly currently uses Cashu tokens and mint-backed wallet operations. Requests advertise accepted mints; an in-band payment carries a token; the recipient attempts redemption and returns a result. The application keeps pending operations and recovery state. This functionality belongs to the application/payment component, not Core rendezvous.
benefit: Send and receive ecash tokens in the conversation; a mint you choose holds the funds.

title: WISP 202: Ark payments via Arkade
implementation: Experimental browser adapter, Arkade SDK 0.4.74; regtest evidence below. New makes a Mainnet wallet on arkade.computer or a Testnet one on Mutinynet, in one click.
summary: This adapter implements Ark payments using @arkade-os/sdk 0.4.74. Ark is the payment method; Arkade is the selected provider implementation. Bark is a second, separate Ark provider: not a separate currency, and not compatible with this one (a Bark wallet cannot pay an Arkade address). Arkade was selected because its TypeScript wallet, transaction preparation, operator/indexer clients and browser repositories fit the
benefit: Review and approve an exact Ark payment through a pinned operator.
note: Experimental. New makes a Mainnet wallet or a Testnet one in one click; payment flows were exercised only on a local regtest network. There is no unilateral exit yet.

title: WISP 203: Lightning
implementation: Several Lightning cards per network, each on its own source (Cashu mints, Fedimint, Breez, NWC, Core Lightning, LND, WebLN)
summary: The current btc-lightning-bolt11 endpoint carries an invoice; the application reaches Lightning through the sources below. This is not evidence of a universal external-wallet adapter. BOLT 11 is the invoice format reference.
benefit: Carry a Lightning invoice in the chat and pay or receive it through the wallet.
note: Several Lightning cards per network, one of them the default for receiving: your Cashu mint or your own node or wallet (NWC, LND, Core Lightning, WebLN in the web app, Breez (with your own API key on Mainnet) or a Fedimint federation). Any other wallet can pay the invoice from its QR code.

title: WISP 204: Ark payments via Bark
implementation: Experimental browser adapter, Second's Bark SDK @secondts/bark 0.25.0 (bark 0.7.1, WebAssembly). New makes a Mainnet wallet on Second's Bitcoin server and a Testnet one on their signet server, each in one click. Regtest evidence below; no Ghostly test has moved real money.
summary: Bark is Second's implementation of Ark: a client (bark) and a server (captaind). This adapter is a second Ark provider beside Arkade 202, and not interchangeable with it. Checked on 2026-09-23 against bark 0.7.1:
benefit: A second Ark provider (Second's Bark) beside Arkade, so Ark isn't tied to one implementation.
note: Experimental. Mainnet on Second's Bitcoin server, Testnet on their signet server; no unilateral exit yet. Not interchangeable with Arkade: its own payment method and capability.

title: WISP 205: Lightning Addresses and LNURL-pay
implementation: Paying a Lightning address or LNURL through a Lightning card; no wire format
summary: A Lightning address (name@domain, LUD-16) or an LNURL (lnurl1…, LUD-01; lnurlp://…, LUD-17) names an HTTPS service that hands out invoices on request (LUD-06). This draft covers paying one from a Ghostly client, in the wallet's Send tab and from an address pasted in a chat. Nothing crosses the data link: the chat carries the address as text, like any invoice. Receiving on a Lightning address needs a server the person
benefit: Pay a Lightning address (name@domain) or an LNURL from the wallet or straight from a chat, through your Lightning source.
note: Paying only: receiving on an address needs a server you run. The domain is named before anything is fetched, and the service must allow cross-origin reads.

title: WISP 2xx: Fedimint ecash and Lightning through a federation
implementation: Experimental browser adapter on the Fedimint web SDK (@fedimint/core canary, pinned). Mainnet and Testnet, each joined by invite code; regtest evidence below (Mainnet not yet exercised with real funds).
summary: Fedimint is a federation of guardians who hold bitcoin together (a threshold of them must agree on everything) and issue blinded ecash for it. It has three modules this adapter uses: mint (ecash notes), ln (Lightning through a gateway, a Lightning node that swaps ecash for HTLCs) and wallet (on-chain peg-in and peg-out, not used here yet). Joining a federation is trusting its guardians with the sats: custodial like a
benefit: Ecash from a federation of guardians you choose: in a chat, and Lightning through the federation's gateway.
note: Experimental, on Mainnet and Testnet; not yet tried with real funds. You see a federation's name, guardians and network before joining. Number not yet assigned.

title: WISP 2xx: Spark payments
implementation: Experimental browser adapter, Breez SDK Spark @breeztech/breez-sdk-spark 0.26.0 (WebAssembly, nodeless). New makes a Testnet wallet on Breez and Lightspark's hosted regtest in one click, and a Mainnet wallet once the person gives their Breez API key.
summary: Spark is a Bitcoin layer 2. Its signing operators co-sign transfers of off-chain leaves: a transfer between two Spark wallets is instant, costs no on-chain fee, and needs no Lightning route. Before this draft Ghostly used Spark only through the Breez Lightning source (203, breez): it paid and received BOLT11 invoices from a Spark wallet. This adapter makes Spark a way of paying of its own, spark. Two contacts who bot
benefit: Pay a contact who also has Spark straight from wallet to wallet: instant, off-chain, no Lightning hop.
note: Experimental: Mainnet with your own Breez API key; Testnet runs on Breez's hosted regtest with no key. The same wallet can be your Lightning source. Number not yet assigned.

title: WISP 300: Identity Proofs
implementation: Identity proofs with a provider contract: Nostr, Pubky, domain, OpenPGP, Bitcoin address, SSH, DID, AT Protocol (Bluesky); OpenID Connect built but not offered (no client ID). See 2026-09-23
summary: External identity is an optional attestation about a participation, not the session's transport or its per-message signer. The providers in use are listed under Providers. A participant may offer multiple proofs or none; local/channel policy decides whether any are required.
benefit: Optionally prove to one contact that you control an outside identity. Never required.
note: Rebuilt on 2026-09-23: a proof is made once in Profile → Identities, shared per chat only when you choose, withdrawable and revocable through a DHT record. Web, desktop, extension and the headless CLI.

title: WISP 301: Nostr
implementation: Nostr identity-proof provider; see 2026-09-23
summary: Optional Nostr proof of a Ghost participation, implemented as the nostr identity provider (below). NIP-01 defines Nostr's signed event structure; it does not define this Ghost proof or reserve a Ghost event kind.
benefit: An optional Nostr proof, and where a signer's authority ends.
note: Signed once with a NIP-07 browser extension (web app, desktop) or a NIP-46 remote signer. A proof, not a transport, and not permission to publish.

title: WISP 3xx: Pubky identity (approved in Pubky Ring or Pubky Passport)
implementation: Identity provider pubky (web, extension, desktop): packages/browser/src/proofs/providers/pubky.ts, proofs/pubky.ts; core pubkyProofs.ts, pkdns.ts
summary: A person shows a contact, optionally and per contact, that they hold a Pubky key: the key Pubky Ring (a phone) or Pubky Passport (a browser) keeps for them. It is a provider of the identity-proof contract (PROOFS.md), id pubky, category self-custodied: made once on the Identities page, then shared per contact through WISP 300's exchange like every other identity.
benefit: Show a contact you hold a Pubky key: approve one request in Pubky Ring or Pubky Passport, and Ghostly writes a small proof file to your homeserver.
note: The proof is published, not signed: Ring and Passport approve Pubky auth requests only. Number not yet assigned.

title: WISP 3xx: Keet
implementation: Blocked on existing-identity signer API; see follow-up
summary: Investigate an optional Keet identity proof. This is a feasibility draft, not a claim that Keet exposes an appropriate signing API, public identity format or bridge. Keet's official site describes the product; it is not evidence of a Ghost integration contract. No local adapter was found.
notices: Planned integration. No current integration is enabled or promised. The historical document identifier 303 remains in the URL for link compatibility; it is not a committed WISP number.
benefit: Investigate an optional relationship with a Keet identity.
note: Blocked until Keet offers a supported signing API for existing accounts; the 2026-09-20 compatible import stays off. Number not yet assigned.

title: WISP 3xx: AT Protocol identity (Bluesky)
implementation: Experimental provider atproto: packages/core/src/atprotoRepo.ts, atprotoIdentity.ts, packages/browser/src/proofs/atproto/, proofs/providers/atproto.ts. Real servers need the client metadata served at ghostly.tools (it ships with the website)
summary: A person shows one contact that they control an AT Protocol account (a Bluesky account, or one on any other Personal Data Server). The evidence is a record in the account's own repository, which the account's key signs; the contact checks it from the repository, without logging in anywhere and without a Ghostly server.
benefit: Show a contact that you control a Bluesky (AT Protocol) account, checked from its signed repository without logging in.
note: Approved once on your own server, asking only for Ghostly's records; the record is public. Built, and offered once the website's OAuth client document is live. Number not yet assigned.

title: WISP 3xx: Bitcoin Address Proof
implementation: Experimental provider bitcoin (packages/browser/src/proofs/providers/bitcoin.ts); verifier in @ghostly/core
summary: An optional proof that the person can sign with the key behind a Bitcoin address. It follows WISP 300's two layers: the person signs, once, in their own wallet, the binding statement by which the address authorizes their Ghostly profile key for a validity window; per chat, the app presents that binding with a presentation signed by the profile key and bound to the chat, the contact and a fresh challenge, without aski
benefit: Prove you hold the key behind a Bitcoin address with one BIP-322 signature from your wallet.
note: Experimental. Checked on the device with no blockchain lookup; proves no balance, past payment or willingness to pay. Number not yet assigned.

title: WISP 3xx: Profile DID (did:dht)
implementation: Experimental, web, desktop and extension: packages/core/src/didDht.ts, packages/browser/src/engine/did.ts, src/components/identities/PublicDid.tsx, Desktop publishsignedpacket
summary: Every Ghostly profile has a W3C Decentralized Identifier of the did:dht method (DIF, specification version 0): a DID document written as DNS records into the Pkarr packet of an Ed25519 key and stored in the Mainline DHT as a BEP44 mutable item, the same mechanism Ghostly uses for chats (01). Any did:dht resolver reads it, with no Ghostly server involved.
benefit: Every profile gets a public identifier of its own, a did:dht that any resolver reads from the DHT, with no Ghostly server.
note: Experimental. Its own key, never a chat's; it lists an identity only when you switch it on. Web, desktop and extension. Number not yet assigned.

title: WISP 3xx: Decentralized identifiers (DIDs)
implementation: Experimental provider did; see below
summary: An optional identity proof, under 300, that a person controls a W3C decentralized identifier. The DID vouches, once, for the WISP 300 binding statement, which authorizes the profile's own proof key for a validity period; each chat the proof is shared with then gets a presentation signed by that proof key (shared WISP 300 machinery, no DID involved). A contact's app resolves the DID itself and checks the evidence agai
benefit: A decentralized identifier (did:key, did:jwk, did:dht or did:web) signs once with one of its keys, or a did:web publishes beside its did.json.
note: Experimental, under Advanced. Each contact resolves the DID again. Number not yet assigned.

title: WISP 3xx: Domain Proofs
implementation: Experimental provider domain: packages/core/src/domainProofs.ts, packages/browser/src/proofs/domain.ts, packages/browser/src/proofs/providers/domain.ts
summary: A person shows a contact that they control a domain name, such as example.com, by publishing a record under it. It is an optional identity proof under 300 and the provider contract: chat works without it, it is shared with one contact at a time, and it says nothing about who holds the domain in law.
benefit: Show a contact that you control a domain, with a DNS record or a file on your site.
note: Experimental. Looked up through a DNS-over-HTTPS resolver the contact chooses and re-checked after a day, so removing the record withdraws the proof. Number not yet assigned.

title: WISP 3xx: Nostr social layer
implementation: Experimental: packages/browser/src/nostr/, packages/browser/src/engine/nostrSocial.ts; see below
summary: What a proven Nostr identity (301 under 300) lets a person show and do in Ghostly, as separate capabilities, each permitted on its own, exactly as the roadmap's layer table separates them:
benefit: What a proven Nostr key lets a contact see (profile, follows, notes) and, if you turn it on, posting through your own signer.
note: Experimental. Loaded only on request, from relays you choose; publishing is off by default and each post is confirmed. Web, desktop and extension (NIP-46 only there). Number not yet assigned.

title: WISP 3xx: Provider-attested identity (OpenID Connect)
implementation: Built, not offered: packages/browser/src/proofs/oidc/, provider oidc. Every client ID in oidc/providers.ts is empty, so no provider is offered or accepted until the maintainer registers them (checklist)
summary: A person shows one contact that an account at a provider (Google, Microsoft, Apple, GitLab, Twitch) signed in for this conversation. The evidence is the provider's own signed ID token; the contact checks it against the provider's published keys. No Ghostly server takes part.
benefit: Show a contact that an account at Google, Microsoft, Apple, GitLab or Twitch signed in for this conversation.
note: Attested by the provider, not a key you hold; the contact trusts that company. Built, but not offered until the maintainer registers Ghostly's OAuth clients. Number not yet assigned.

title: WISP 3xx: OpenPGP
implementation: Provider openpgp in the identity-proof registry; see Implementation
summary: An optional proof that a participant controls an OpenPGP key (RFC 9580, and the RFC 4880 v4 keys people already have). The participant signs a Ghostly statement with their own tooling (gpg --clearsign, or gpg --detach-sign --armor) and gives the result and their public key to their app. Ghostly never holds the secret key, so the same flow works when the key lives on a YubiKey or another OpenPGP card: gpg asks for the
benefit: Sign the statement once with your own gpg (a YubiKey works unchanged), and the contact verifies it locally.
note: Holding a key proves nothing about the name or email in its user ID, and the app says so. Number not yet assigned.

title: WISP 3xx: SSH keys
implementation: Experimental providers ssh, ssh-github, ssh-gitlab; see below
summary: An optional identity proof, under 300, that a person controls an SSH key. The key signs, once, the WISP 300 binding statement, which authorizes the profile's own proof key for a validity period; each chat the proof is shared with then gets a presentation signed by that proof key (shared WISP 300 machinery, no SSH involved). A contact's app verifies both locally. Variants prove a GitHub or GitLab account instead of a
benefit: An SSH key signs once with ssh-keygen; a GitHub or GitLab account counts through the keys it publishes.
note: Experimental. Never grants a server login. Number not yet assigned.

title: WISP 400: Chat Messaging
implementation: The single layered chat of revision 0.2 in every new chat (web, extension, desktop): first contact on the DHT and a stream in parallel, on-dht, self-upgrade, DHT only per chat; replies, reactions, edits and the text's display conventions; compatibility chats for v0.4
summary: There is one kind of 1:1 chat and one invite format. Every chat has two layers:
benefit: One chat for everyone: the DHT to meet, a live link when one connects, the DHT again when none does.
note: Messages with storage receipts and retries. A first pairing with no direct path starts on the DHT, short texts fall back to it when a live link drops, and every chat returns to a live link by itself. You can keep a chat on the DHT only. Replies quote a message, a text you sent can be edited, in a chat or a group, reactions put one emoji per person on a message, and lists, quotes, headings and links show as such.

title: WISP 401: Chat Session
implementation: The layer-1 session of every new chat (paired-chat/1): WebRTC, and native Iroh/HyperDHT where supported. First contact on the DHT in parallel, and automatic upgrade; calls (calls/1, screen sharing inside a call), shared apps (services/1), files/3, the typing indicator (typing/1), reactions (react/1) and edits (edit/1) on the live session; replies on texts and files.
summary: This is the layer-1 session of the one chat of 400. Formerly "paired chat", it is no longer a kind of chat the person picks: every new chat is a paired-chat/1 chat, whose layer 0 is the DHT (403) and whose layer 1 is this session, when a transport connects. The wire identifiers (paired-chat/1, chat/1, the frame names) are unchanged.
benefit: The live session of every chat: pinned keys, a durable outbox, names and pictures, over WebRTC, Iroh or HyperDHT.
note: Every new chat on web, desktop and extension, calls included while it is live. The typing indicator goes over the live session only, and each person can turn it off.

title: WISP 402: Compatibility Chat (v0.4 Timestamp Profile)
implementation: Legacy 1:1 clients (v0.4 and earlier, the Rust CLI) and the read/write path kept in current apps; the compatibility header and Continue in a new chat in current apps
summary: Formerly "Legacy Timestamp Chat". This profile is not withdrawn: withdrawing it would cut off every contact still on Ghostly 0.4 and every chat made with it. It is retained for compatibility with a narrowed scope:
benefit: Chats with Ghostly 0.4 contacts keep working, calls included. A new chat never uses it.

title: WISP 403: DHT Text
implementation: The floor and first contact of every new chat (web, extension, desktop); DHT only per chat; pinned mailboxes. Native clients read the Mainline DHT directly; browsers go through Pkarr relays.
summary: This profile is the floor of every chat of 400: the delivery that works whenever both sides reach the DHT, whatever else fails. It carries:
benefit: The floor of every chat: very short text through DHT records when no live link is up. Bounded, not a mailbox.
note: 256 bytes, retried for five minutes: the first contact of every chat, after a live link drops, or in a chat set to DHT only. Chats with 0.4 contacts: up to 500 bytes (WISP 402).

title: WISP 4xx: Store-and-Forward for an Away Contact
implementation: Experimental: hold/1 in web, extension and desktop clients; exercised against a local S3-compatible server
summary: Without this profile, a message for a contact who is away reaches them only as short text through bounded DHT records (403); a picture or a payment request waits until both are online (401). This profile lets what is sent meanwhile be held (text, a small file, a payment request) and delivered when the contact is back, with bounds that are stated rather than implied. Nothing here replaces the paired session or the DHT
benefit: Text, a picture or a payment request sent while a contact is away waits, sealed, in your own S3 bucket and reaches them when they are back.
note: Experimental, in chats with the switch on at both ends; web, desktop and extension. Picked up until seven days after you were last online. Ecash is never held. Number not yet assigned.

title: WISP 500: File Transfer
implementation: 1:1 transfer in every chat: files/3 (any size) and files/2 on the chat session (501), held files while not live (4xx), 502 frames in compatibility chats
summary: In the one chat of 400, a file (a voice message included) travels over layer 1 with 501, or, while the chat is not live, in a hold (4xx, at most 8 MiB) when both sides allow it. It never travels in DHT records, split or whole: the floor of 403 carries text only. With neither available, the file waits in the sender's outbox with a cancel ("Sends when live") and goes when layer 1 is back. Queued files count against the
benefit: Send a file straight to a contact, checked and acknowledged on arrival.
note: Any size, with both people online; above 25 MB the receiver accepts first, and a transfer resumes where it stopped. Chats with 0.4 contacts: up to 100 MiB.

title: WISP 501: Chat Files
implementation: Every chat session: files/3 (any size, consent, resume) and files/2 for older apps; WebRTC and supported native adapters
summary: Formerly "Paired Files". This is how files travel in every chat of 400 while it is live. The wire (files/2, pf- frames) is unchanged. While the chat is on-dht or dht-chosen, files are held (4xx) or wait in the outbox for layer 1 (500); a files/2 transfer cut by a drop to the DHT fails and is retried whole when layer 1 is back, under its original ID; a files/3 transfer resumes from what was stored (below).
benefit: How files travel in every chat: negotiated, chunk by chunk, with integrity checks.

title: WISP 502: Compatibility File Frames
implementation: Compatibility chats' live data links; both peers online.
summary: Formerly "Legacy File Frames". Retained, not withdrawn: a compatibility chat (402) with a contact on Ghostly 0.4 still sends and receives files this way over its legacy WebRTC link. A new chat uses 501 only. The number and file name stay.
benefit: File frames of chats with Ghostly 0.4 contacts, so they can still send and receive files.

title: WISP 600: Voice and Video
implementation: 1:1 calls, with screen sharing from inside a call, in every chat: compatibility chats (call) and the chat session (calls/1, live only)
summary: This document defines common responsibilities and proposed extensions. Exact implemented encodings and runtime limits belong to 601 · WebRTC Media. Supporting a concrete profile does not establish full conformance to this Draft.
benefit: Voice, video and screen sharing, coordinated apart from the data stream.
note: In every chat while it is live, the Linux desktop included (with media of its own, its webview having no WebRTC). Not in groups.

title: WISP 601: WebRTC Media
implementation: Compatibility chats (call) and the chat session of every new chat (calls/1); capture varies by platform. Desktop on Linux runs WebRTC in Rust and media in GStreamer (#331), with no screen sharing yet.
summary: The implemented 1:1 profile uses compact call signaling and live call control frames, with ICE/fingerprint/candidate validation and a freshness window. Its v2 behavior pre-negotiates video so camera/screen changes can use replaceTrack; picture state is signaled separately. Call signal validation and the protocol define exact fields and legacy compatibility.
benefit: One-to-one calls over WebRTC media, with compact call signaling.
note: Screen sharing needs a computer; phone browsers can't share a screen.

title: WISP 700: Local Services
implementation: Existing HTTP proxy, in every chat (desktop and extension hosts)
summary: This document defines common responsibilities and proposed extensions. Exact implemented encodings and runtime limits belong to 701 · HTTP Local Service Profile. Supporting a concrete profile does not establish full conformance to this Draft.
benefit: Let chosen contacts open an app or site running on your computer, while you are online.
note: Desktop app and extension, at both ends; not the web app. You choose which contacts see each app.

title: WISP 701: HTTP Local Service Profile
implementation: Desktop/extension hosting in every chat: data-link frames in compatibility chats, the same frames inside ph frames in the chat session (services/1); web viewer where supported.
summary: Control req frames carry request ID, service ID, method, path, sanitized headers and body presence. res carries status/headers/body presence; bounded binary chunks carry bodies and rst cancels/resets. Reject unknown/disabled/unauthorized service IDs, invalid methods/headers, target escape, excess body/concurrency and idle timeout. Do not inherit the host's cookies or local credentials.
benefit: HTTP requests and responses carried over the chat's data link.
note: Plain request/response. No WebSockets or streaming.

title: WISP 800: Invite and Join
implementation: One bearer invite (ghostly1…) for every new chat, which pins the inviter's participation key; consumable admission protocol proposed
summary: Every new 1:1 chat starts from the same invite (801): one bech32m string, ghostly1…, also shareable as https://ghostly.tools/#ghostly1…. The invite no longer chooses how the chat is carried; the handshake does, on the DHT and on a stream in parallel (400). Its format version is the first data symbol, and the error rules go both ways: a current app answers a newer version with "Update to join", a failed checksum with
benefit: Turn a private invitation into a mutually admitted connection.

title: WISP 801: Implemented Invitation Profiles
implementation: Every current app creates only ghostly1… codes and links, and reads by the rules below (pair1/, pair2d/ and v0.4 codes still accepted as input)
summary: A current app creates exactly one kind of invite, for the one chat of 400. There is no "Live chat" or "Text only" choice: how the chat is carried is decided after the handshake, and can be changed per chat at any time.
benefit: The invitation formats clients actually produce: links, QR codes and connection strings.
note: One ghostly1… code, checked for typos, shared as text, a QR code or a ghostly.tools link that opens the app. Older codes are still read.

title: WISP 900: Group Session Negotiation
implementation: Two profiles: group-mesh/1 (private, up to eight) and group-community/1 (a link anyone can open, hundreds of members, admission by any member); core, engine, UI, e2e and a headless load test; text with @mentions, a group picture and payments between members
summary: Define how a group of Ghostly peers agrees on who is in it, protects what they say across membership changes, and moves it between them without touching Pkarr/DHT. Revision 0.1 was a proposal with every choice open. Revision 0.2 recorded the choices made for the first distribution profile, 9xx · Group Mesh. Revision 0.3 adds a second, 9xx · Group Community, for the group whose link is the way in: posted in a large co
benefit: How a group agrees on who is in it, locks out whoever left, and moves messages between members, never through the DHT.
note: Two profiles implemented: group-mesh/1 (private, up to eight members, one admin) and group-community/1 (a link anyone can open, up to 256). Text, a picture and payments between members; web, desktop and extension.

title: WISP 9xx: GossipSub Transport
implementation: Proposed; no adapter found
summary: Evaluate GossipSub as an off-DHT distribution layer for group sessions. No Ghostly adapter was found. libp2p GossipSub v1.1 describes mesh/gossip routing and peer scoring; neither routing nor scoring is group encryption, membership consensus or guaranteed storage.
notices: Planned integration. No current integration is enabled or promised. The historical document identifier 901 remains in the URL for link compatibility; it is not a committed WISP number.
benefit: Evaluate GossipSub as a distribution layer for groups larger than the mesh.
note: A later profile, after the mesh is measured; no adapter. Number not yet assigned.

title: WISP 9xx: Group Community Distribution Profile
implementation: group-community/1: core protocol in groupCommunity.ts and communityRendezvous.ts; engine in community.ts, payments in communityPay.ts; UI shared with the mesh; unit tests, a six-browser e2e, a three-browser payments e2e and a headless load test
summary: A group whose link is the way in: posted in a large community, anyone who opens it joins, whether or not the admin is online, and the group holds hundreds of members, not eight. group-mesh/1 stays what it is (a small private group of contacts); a group says which of the two it is from its first commit, and never changes.
benefit: A group whose link is the way in: anyone who opens it joins, any member lets them in while the admin is away, up to 256 members.
note: Text, a picture and payments, sealed to the two members and carried by the hubs. Online members elect a few hubs that relay; whoever was away is caught up by whoever is there. The cap is what a headless load test measured. Number not yet assigned.

title: WISP 9xx: Group Mesh Distribution Profile
implementation: group-mesh/1: core protocol in packages/core and, for the group's link (group-entry/1), groupEntry.ts; engine, UI and four-browser e2e in packages/browser and e2e/web/groups.spec.ts; web, extension and desktop share it
summary: Payments between two members are part of it (§ Payments): the money travels on their edge, the group sees a note. Files, media, calls and local services are not part of this profile and are refused in groups.
benefit: Up to eight people, each pair on its own authenticated link, with a fresh group key whenever someone joins or leaves.
note: Text, a picture set by the admin, and payments between two members over their own link; files and calls are refused in groups. A member who was away catches up from each author's recent messages. Number not yet assigned.
